Today's Focus

How was a globalized world made, and what did it gain and cost?

The phone in your pocket may have been designed in California, built from parts made on three continents, and assembled in Asia. Today you will see how such a world was made, who gained and who lost, and what Europe tried to build after its wars. Keep this week's discussion question in mind: is globalization uniting or dividing the world?

Objectives
  1. Describe how trade, technology, and political change tied the world's economies more closely together after 1945.
  2. Explain how European integration began with the Schuman Declaration and grew into the European Union.
  3. Evaluate the gains and strains that globalization brought to different peoples.
Quick Check-in

The phone in your pocket may have been designed in California, built from parts made on three continents, and assembled in Asia. Before you read: what do you expect made such a world possible?

⚡ DECIDE FIRST
It is 1947, and you are a trade minister. Your country's shirt mills employ thousands of people in a small town. Foreign shirts could be sold here for a fraction of the price if [[term:tariff|tariffs]] came down. You must decide whether to join an agreement to lower [[term:tariff|tariffs]] together.
Decide first, and jot your answer in your notebook: what would you do, and who would pay for it? Then open to compare.
The lesson shows what twenty-three countries chose in 1947: to lower [[term:tariff|tariffs]] step by step, remembering how trade collapsed in the 1930s when nations raised them. It also names the trade-off. Shoppers can buy more for less, but a worker whose job can be done more cheaply abroad may lose it. Other paths were open, such as lowering [[term:tariff|tariffs]] on some goods and keeping them on others, and the lesson does not claim that any one course was certain to work. Weigh the town's mills against the buyers of the shirts, and keep your answer for the discussion.
⚡ WEIGHING THE RECORD
People moved across borders in huge numbers after 1945. How would you describe the record of that movement?

    A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science

    Part 1

    Trade Without Walls

    Chapter 1Trade Without Walls
    Chapter 1

    Trade Without Walls

    The leaders who built the postwar order remembered the 1930s, when nations raised tariffs and trade collapsed. In 1947 twenty-three countries signed an agreement, called GATT, to lower tariffs step by step. In 1995 it became the World Trade Organization. The cost of moving goods also fell. In 1956 an American trucker named Malcom McLean sent a ship with fifty-eight truck bodies packed in its hold. His idea, the shipping container, let a crate be lifted from a ship to a train to a truck without being opened. Loading costs dropped sharply, and it became cheap to make goods far from where they were sold. The growing connection of the world's economies is called globalization.

    Trade needed stable money as well. In July 1944 delegates meeting at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, set up the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank so that countries would have a steady system of exchange to trade within. The container changed the other side of the bargain. Before it, cargo was loaded piece by piece, in sacks, barrels, and crates carried aboard by gangs of dockworkers, and a ship could sit in port for days. McLean's own figures put the cost of loading a ton at about six dollars by the old method and about sixteen cents by container. Standard sizes soon followed, so that a box filled in one country would fit any ship, train, or truck in another. Lower tariffs made foreign goods cheaper to sell, and cheaper shipping made them cheaper to buy.

    Economists have long argued that trade lets each region make what it makes best, so that everyone can buy more for less. A shirt sewn in one country from cotton grown in another, and sold in a third, can cost a fraction of what it would cost if each country made everything for itself. Adam Smith had made this argument in 1776. The same logic also means that a worker whose job can be done more cheaply abroad may lose that job, a trade-off you will weigh in the discussion.

    Political change added to the trend. When communism collapsed in Europe, a vast area opened to trade. In 1978 China, under Deng Xiaoping, began to allow markets, and it joined the World Trade Organization in 2001. Within a generation its economy grew from a poor farming land into the world's workshop. In 1991 India dropped many controls on its economy, and it, too, began to grow fast. These changes lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty, which is among the greatest gains in human history.

    China's first steps were small. In the late 1970s the government let farm families work plots for themselves and sell what they grew beyond a set amount to the state, and harvests rose. In 1980 it opened a special zone at Shenzhen, then a fishing town beside Hong Kong, where foreign firms could build factories under few rules. Shenzhen grew into a city of millions. Markets did not bring political freedom. When students and workers gathered in Tiananmen Square in Beijing in the spring of 1989 to demand reform, the army cleared the square by force on June 4. India's change came out of a crisis. By mid-1991 the country had hardly enough foreign money in reserve to pay for a few weeks of imports. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao and his finance minister, Manmohan Singh, ended the system of licenses that had required government permission to start or expand a factory, and they cut tariffs. The World Bank reckons that in 1990 about a third of humanity lived in extreme poverty, and that by 2019 fewer than one person in ten did.

    Part 2

    A New Kind of Europe

    Chapter 2A New Kind of Europe
    Chapter 2

    A New Kind of Europe

    Europe's leaders drew a different lesson from the wars that had ravaged their continent. On May 9, 1950, the French foreign minister Robert Schuman, in a speech you will read, proposed that France and West Germany place their coal and steel production under a common authority open to other nations. Coal and steel were the stuff of weapons, so such a pact would make war between the two "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible." Schuman and his adviser Jean Monnet had a plan, and Konrad Adenauer, the German chancellor, and others agreed. In 1951 six nations, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg, formed the European Coal and Steel Community.

    Seventy years of grievance lay behind the proposal. France and Germany had fought in 1870, in 1914, and in 1939, and the border region of Alsace and Lorraine had changed hands among them. The Ruhr valley, where Germany's coal and steel came from, was the arsenal of each of those wars. Schuman did not promise a united Europe at once. "Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single plan," he said. It would be built, he went on, through concrete achievements that first created a solidarity among peoples. The treaty of 1951 set up a High Authority, whose members did not take orders from any single government, to oversee both countries' coal and steel. It took effect in 1952.

    The six widened their cooperation in 1957 with a common market, and over the decades more nations joined. In 1992 the Maastricht Treaty created the European Union, and in 2002 most members adopted a common currency, the euro. Citizens could live and work in any member state. Yet the Union has also met resistance. Many voters feel that decisions are made by distant officials, and in 2016 Britain voted to leave. The Union is neither a nation nor a simple alliance, and Europeans still disagree about what it should become.

    Part 3

    People on the Move

    Chapter 3People on the Move
    Chapter 3

    People on the Move

    People moved as freely as goods, and often more painfully. After the war, former colonies sent workers to Britain, France, and the Netherlands. West Germany invited guest workers from Turkey and southern Europe. Millions moved from poor countries to richer ones, seeking work and safety, and by 2020 about one person in thirty lived outside the country of their birth. Migration filled jobs and enriched cultures, but it also caused fierce arguments over borders, jobs, language, and identity. Some migrants fled war, among them millions from Syria after 2011, and the numbers strained many nations.

    Germany signed an agreement with Turkey in 1961 to bring in workers, who were called guest workers because both sides expected them to go home. Many stayed and sent for their families. The Swiss writer Max Frisch is remembered for the line, "We asked for workers, and human beings came." In Britain a ship, the Empire Windrush, brought about five hundred workers from the Caribbean in 1948, the first of many who came as subjects of the empire. The money that migrants sent home to their relatives now adds up to more than all the foreign aid that governments give, according to the World Bank.

    The movement of money, ideas, and fear also crossed borders. The attacks of 2001 showed that terrorism could strike far from its source, and the global financial crisis of 2008 began with bad loans in America and quickly harmed banks and families on every continent. Globalization linked fortunes together, for good and for ill.

    The crisis of 2008 shows how the links worked. American banks had lent money for houses to borrowers who could not repay, then bundled the loans into securities and sold them to banks and investors around the world. When homeowners began to default, no one knew which institutions held the losses. In September 2008 the American investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed, lending between banks froze, and a recession spread to Europe and Asia. Governments rushed to rescue banks, and many people lost jobs and homes.

    Part 4

    Science and Technology

    Chapter 4Science and Technology
    Chapter 4

    Science and Technology

    Science brought some of the sharpest changes. In the 1960s Norman Borlaug, an American scientist working in Mexico and India, helped develop wheat and rice that yielded far more grain. This Green Revolution is credited with saving a large number of people from famine. A worldwide campaign wiped out smallpox, which had killed hundreds of millions in the twentieth century, and the last natural case occurred in 1977. In 2003 scientists finished mapping the human genome, the full set of instructions in human cells. Average life expectancy around the world rose from about forty-six years in 1950 to more than seventy by the early 2020s.

    Borlaug's wheat succeeded because of a change in the shape of the plant. Older varieties grew tall, and when they were fed with fertilizer they put out heavy heads of grain that bent the stalks until they fell over and rotted. The new short-stemmed varieties could carry the extra grain, and together with fertilizer and irrigation they raised harvests sharply in Mexico, India, and Pakistan. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. Smallpox gave way to a method more than two centuries old, the vaccination that Edward Jenner had shown in 1796 protected against the disease. In the 1960s and 1970s teams of health workers traveled from village to village, finding each case and vaccinating everyone around it, until the last natural case turned up in Somalia in 1977. The World Health Organization declared the disease gone in 1980.

    Communication changed even faster. The first message passed between two computers in 1969. In 1989 a British scientist, Tim Berners-Lee, proposed the World Wide Web, and by 1991 it was running. Within a generation, billions of people were online, able to share information in seconds. In 2020 a new virus, COVID-19, spread around the world in weeks, aided by air travel. Scientists then designed effective vaccines in less than a year, which was only possible because researchers in many nations shared data.

    That first message in 1969 went from a computer at the University of California, Los Angeles, to one at Stanford. The operator meant to type the word "login," and the receiving machine crashed after the first two letters, so the first message was "lo." The network had been built to link a few research computers. Berners-Lee wrote his proposal at CERN, the European physics laboratory, to help scientists find one another's papers, and CERN later made the Web's software free for anyone to use. When COVID-19 appeared, Chinese scientists published the virus's genetic code in January 2020, and laboratories everywhere began work on vaccines within weeks. The first were approved for use in December.

    Part 5

    Uniting or Dividing

    Chapter 5Uniting or Dividing
    Chapter 5

    Uniting or Dividing

    The internet itself carries both effects. It lets a student in a small town read the same books as one in a great city, and it lets a hidden network plan an attack or spread a lie as quickly as a doctor can share a cure. Tools do not decide how they are used. People do.

    The gains were real, and so were the costs. Factory towns in older industrial nations lost jobs when production moved abroad, and some communities have never recovered. Competition from abroad pushed wages down in some trades, and some countries, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, gained little. Others worry that local customs and languages are being drowned by a global culture. Meanwhile, new powers, led by China, challenge the position the United States has held since 1945.

    Neither a rosy view nor a gloomy one fits the record. For centuries, from the Roman roads to the Atlantic trade you studied earlier, people have tied the world together, and the pattern has often brought wealth along with conflict. History offers no law that says what comes next. Nations and their leaders will keep making choices, and those choices will depend on the character of citizens as much as on markets and machines. You have now followed the story from the fall of Rome to the present. In your discussion, weigh what you have learned and decide what you think.
